data.title: Gen Z helped Democrats win. Now it may want new leadership
data.description:
Gen Z delivered a decisive win for Democrats in the 2026 midterm elections. Now they may want to see change in party leadership.  

Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), who has led Senate Democrats since 2017, is facing achallenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) to become majority leader in the Democratic-controlled 120th Congress. 

Van Hollen is the progressive in the race, and is getting support from the left,including from Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.).

Gen Z activists The Hill spoke with particularly emphasized a desire for change. They see the leadership race as an opportunity to get fresh blood atop the party.

Peter McKenzie, a 26-year-old member of the progressive veteran group Common Defense, said people believe “a new majority needs a new approach.”

Dakota Hall, executive director of Alliance for Youth Action (AYA), voiced similar thoughts.

“People across the board want big, not small, change right now,” he said. “Democrats won these voters because they had the change vehicle on the ballot a couple weeks ago, and if they stop being that, these voters will leave.”

He said he can see this in Gen Z’s view of Schumer.

“They’re most skeptical about Chuck due to his ties to the establishment. This election was a turning of the page of this country, where young people want to see a whole crop of new leaders,” he added.

Schumer has been a longtime supporter of Israel, who opposed the Obama-era Iran nuclear deal. He’s become a critic of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, but Van Hollen has him on Israel, for accepting money from PACs, and for opposing progressive candidates El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan in primary battles. El-Sayed won his primary and the general election, as did Flanagan in Minnesota. Both are now supporting Van Hollen.

Gen Z is also less likely to support Israel, Gallup data shows, making this Van Hollen point stick out for younger people. Although Van Hollen ran as a pro-Israel Democrat as recently as 2016, he has evolved into a harsh critic of the country’s government since the Gaza war.

A willingness to change is another way to draw Gen Z in. Alex Edgar, founder of AWE Strategies, a consulting firm focused on engaging young people, did not say who he supports for majority leader, but he did say these elections are a way to show young Americans that the party is willing to change. 

“Regardless of who becomes Senate majority leader, you can count on the fact that young people are going to pay attention to the types of policies that are prioritized in the coming years,” he said. “We are looking for leaders who are willing to take a stand and work to create an American dream again for young people.”

Polling doesn’t definitively show who Gen Z would prefer to lead the Senate majority.

A post-Election Day poll from The Economist/YouGov found that Generation Z has a more favorable view of Van Hollen than older Americans. Twenty-eight percent of respondents aged 18-29 held a favorable opinion of Van Hollen, compared to 18 percent of those aged 30-44, 14 percent of those 45-64 and 19 percent of respondents 65 and older. 

Meanwhile, 24 percent of respondents 18-29 said they held a favorable opinion of Schumer, while 33 percent said they held an unfavorable opinion of the long-time New York senator. 

Given the role Gen Z voters played in the Democratic midterm wins two weeks ago, perhaps the surprising thing about the polling is that Schumer is doing better with young Americans polled than older Americans.

More than 50 percent of Millennials, Gen Xers and Boomers reported holding an unfavorable opinion of Schumer.

Van Hollen also faces some challenges, as he’s less known than Schumer, a veteran politician who was lampooned on “Saturday Night Live” after the midterm elections.

Fifty-four percent of those in Generation Z said they “don’t know” how he would lead the Senate.

In March 2025, youth political organizationscalled out Schumer in a letter, titled “Gen Z to Schumer: Fight for Us or Step Aside,” for his leadership as Senate minority leader, saying it was “failing to meet the moment.”

The letter was signed by organizations including the Sunrise Movement, College Democrats of America, Gen Z Against Trump, United We Dream Action and Voters of Tomorrow after Schumer voted to pass a GOP-backed funding bill.  

Members of Gen Z, notably, aren’t eligible to serve in the Senate yet, but that doesn’t mean they don’t pay attention to Senate politics. 

The Economist/YouGov poll found that adults 18-29 are more likely to view Congress as the most powerful branch of government, and they have more faith in the institution than other generations. 

While attitudes toward Congress’s effectiveness are low across the board, 12 percent of Gen Z respondents expressed a “great deal of confidence” in the legislative branch, compared to 6 percent of Millennials, 4 percent of Gen X and 3 percent of Boomers. 

“This is striking such a nerve right now because the election was all about the status quo and the ways in which our current government has been failing so many Americans,” Edgar said. “The Republican and Democratic Parties are both in a position in which they have to earn the votes of their constituents.”

The Feed is a weekly scoop on Generation Z put together by three Generation Z editors at The Hill. We’re working to understand the ins and outs of our generation’s politics. Send tips or comments to awalker@thehill.com, jfeldstein@thehill.com or cleibowitz@thehill.com.

data.title: The Memo: Embattled Trump seeks reset with White House news conference
data.description:
President Trump will seek a reset of sorts when he holds a press conference at the White House at noon EST Friday.

Trump will appear in front of the media after being weakened by the major beating the GOP took in the midterm elections; while the war on Iran stands unresolved; and as he and his allies face uncertainty — and a spate of Democratic-led investigations — during the remaining two years of his presidency.

Even someone with Trump’s ability to shape the media narrative will struggle to turn the page on all those things. But he seems sure to try.

Trump announced the event via a social media post Thursday as he returned from what he termed a “Highly Consequential Trip” to Asia.

He framed the news conference as an opportunity to talk about trade deals with nations in the region. But virtually nobody expects those agreements to be the main focus.

“I imagine it will be more of the same from him [on trade]. That they had a wonderful meeting and reached a bunch of deals that he will have little to no details on,” Stephanie Grisham, who served as White House press secretary and communications director for about nine months of Trump’s first term, told this column. 

Grisham, who is now often critical of the president, predicted that Trump would also play down the recent cascade of tech outages that have caused public disquiet and that he might “blame the midterms on cheating and the Iran war that people ‘just won’t understand had to happen.’”

Trump surprised some observers by accepting the outcome of the midterms at first, even as Democrats easily took the majority in the House and flipped nine Senate seats for a 56-44 majority. The Senate gain, finalized this week with a Democratic victory in a close race in Alaska, was the largest since 1958.

The president fired off a social media post on Nov. 9 questioning whether anyone could “really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest,” however. That message received conspicuously little traction. The response from conservative commentator Megyn Kelly — “Just stop” — was indicative of widespread reluctance to take such claims seriously.

The Friday press conference will, at a minimum, allow Trump to create headlines and, perhaps, to sketch a path forward on some of the issues that loom large in the public mind. As ever, it is also possible the biggest news could come from some entirely unexpected direction.

The GOP’s defeat at the polls was largely driven by Trump’s low popularity ratings, which are in turn a consequence of the unpopular war and a perceived failure to address the cost of living. The two topics are linked given that gas prices, though lower than their peak, remain elevated from prewar levels.

There is speculation about what comes next in Iran, thanks in part to the president’s mixed signals. 

“We don’t need a deal with Iran,” he wrote on social media last week, seeming to suggest that he saw continuing economic pressure on the Islamic Republic as the best way to try to extract further concessions from Tehran. But another American aircraft carrier, the USS Roosevelt, arrived in the Middle East this week, keeping military options open. 

The New York Times reported Wednesday that Trump was mulling “extensive” new strikes on Iran, in part because he was “considering warnings from Israel about Iran’s success in rebuilding its missile and drone arsenals.” 

Such an escalation would be highly contentious at home, though Trump may believe it could help deliver the kind of victory that has eluded him so far.

The president’s lagging poll numbers are also widely viewed as a sign of public weariness with his penchant for self-aggrandizement and chaos — including his controversial plans for the renovation of existing Washington landmarks and the construction of new ones in his honor. 

Trump has given some characteristically mixed signals as to where he intends to go from here in the remaining two years of his presidency. 

In an interview with CBS’s “60 Minutes” right after the midterms, he admitted that his immigration enforcement actions have come to be seen as “too tough” by some people. Yet he also announced the promotion of Stephen Miller, perhaps the most hard-line member of the administration on immigration matters, to replace the departing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.

“Trump has indicated through [elevating] Stephen Miller that he is ready to fight,” GOP strategist Ron Bonjean said. “At the same time, he has been complimentary of Democrats and deferential to them winning power. I think he is going to engage — or there is going to be one heck of a fight coming.”

To be sure, Trump has some political strengths on which he can draw. Even if more Republicans are now privately willing to express misgivings with his leadership in the wake of the midterms, few are inclined to do so publicly — a reminder of the firm grip he continues to exert on his party. 

Even amid his low poll ratings, he retains the avid support of the roughly one-third of Americans who are firmly in the MAGA camp.

In terms of tactics, Trump seems likely to try to defy efforts by the new Democratic majorities to pump the brakes on his agenda. Many of his most sweeping actions have come by the use of executive power rather than through the legislative process, and that is likely to continue.

Allies in the White House — and further afield — are set to do their utmost to frustrate Democratic investigations, too. 

Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, on Monday wrote to incoming House Oversight and Government Reform Committee Chair Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) warning him to preserve documents. Reitz also asserted that “a committee’s gavel is not a prosecutor’s commission.”

There’s one more element of Friday’s news conference that will be closely watched: whether Trump tips his hand in terms of whom he currently favors to succeed him.

The ebbs and flows in the perceived fortunes of Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in particular, have become something of a Beltway obsession in this regard.

The 2028 speculation is a reminder that the post-Trump era is not so far away. But on Friday, it’s only Trump who will be center stage.

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

data.title: Rubio gains buzz while Vance's fortunes falter in GOP race
data.description:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio is up and Vice President Vance is down when it comes to talk about the GOP presidential race.

Rubio is generating growing buzz among Republicans as a potential 2028 presidential contender as the party looks for a savior in the aftermath of a midterm blitz by Democrats, who won 56 seats in the Senate and at least 257 House seats.

The shellacking was widely seen as a repudiation of President Trump and has Republicans wondering if anyone closely aligned with the president, including Rubio, can win a race in 2028 against an ascendant Democratic Party.

Vance blamed the Iran war on the GOP losses a day after the elections, which led to criticism of the vice president in some GOP circles. It may also have made Trump unhappy. The president initially brushed off Vance’s remarks, but he’s also pointedly said the vice president should have said it was the right decision to go to Iran for U.S. security.

Now people close to Vance are sending the signal that he may not run at all for the presidency in 2028. There are also serious questions about whether Rubio will actually run, even as there appear to be growing calls to draft him into the race.

The reason is simple: Rubio is increasingly viewed as someone who could appeal to the party’s base while also attracting a wider coalition, having cultivated a political identity of his own even while serving in one of the Trump administration’s most prominent roles.

Rubio was a rising GOP star in the Tea Party era before becoming a Republican senator from Florida. He ran for president himself in 2016, memorably clashing with Trump on the debate stage.

But even as his standing in the party gains steam, questions are coming up about whether Rubio actually wants to mount another presidential campaign, particularly in an election that some in the GOP see as a difficult cycle for their party.

Some Rubio allies say a White House bid could carry more political risks than rewards, as Republicans grapple with their midterm losses and the future direction of a party that has been dominated by Trump for a decade.

Where MAGA goes after Trump on foreign policy, trade and a host of other issues is very much in play.

Rubio allies suggest it may benefit the Floridian to sit out the 2028 contest, spend time in the private sector and reemerge in 2032 as a presidential candidate. 

His political calculations are also complicated by the president himself, who is expected to loom large over the race to succeed him. The fear for Rubio and other would-be contenders is that they wouldn’t be given enough breathing room to maneuver away from Trump’s positions and rhetoric.

It’s a problem Vance is already experiencing with the Iran war. He was seen as the conflict’s biggest internal critic, but his postelection criticism of the war was not well received in some GOP circles.

Rubio has walked the tightrope with Trump successfully, but it would be a narrow rope indeed as a GOP presidential candidate.

“There are a lot of unknowns, that’s the biggest problem,” said one Rubio ally, who also noted that the secretary of State has yet to sit down with his tight-knit inner circle to discuss any future plans. 

One reason for the uncertainty, according to one former Trump aide, is that the president has asked Rubio to remain in the administration longer. Starting a presidential campaign while serving as secretary of State and national security adviser is a difficult trick.

Still, the former aide argued that Rubio is in the strongest position among other would-be rivals to win the GOP’s presidential nomination, including Vance, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas) and former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin. 

“I think the midterms have changed everyone’s calculus, and Rubio is best positioned to actually win in 2028, where Vance, Cruz and even DeSantis, who I think is the best conservative governor in the past 50 years, would all get smoked,” the former Trump aide said. 

The former aide opined that Rubio would perform better in a presidential race in 2028 than someone outside the administration because he is a part of Trump World and would be better positioned to bring the party together. 

“Because at the end of the day, the party will need to unify to have any chance at winning,” the aide added. “Rubio having that connective tissue with the president, but also the credibility for the folks who are desperate to move on puts him in the best actual position to see that unification happen. Right now there are 10 different factions, [and] Rubio is the best bridge for them all.” 

Jason Cabel Roe, who served as a national spokesperson for Rubio’s 2016 presidential campaign, also said Rubio could fare the best among Republicans. 

“I don’t think there’s any disputing that there is a very wide lane for him,” Cabel Roe said. “I think he’s demonstrated his skill set as Secretary of State, and … I think executed that as well as any member of the Trump Cabinet, without seeming to own a lot of the Trump liabilities.” 

At the same time, some longtime Rubio allies acknowledge it will be an uphill climb for any Republican — much less a Republican who worked in the Trump administration — to win in 2028. 

“On some level, I’m sure he wants to run, but I know there would have to be an obvious path if he were to get in,” one Rubio ally said. “And I’m not sure there is one.” 

Though the midterms were a rebuke of Trump, Republicans expect the president will keep his grip on the party as they select his successor. 

Trump has floated both Vance and Rubio as potential presidential candidates and even suggested a joint Vance-Rubio ticket.

“Regardless of how the midterms turned out, Trump has great influence over who the next Republican presidential nominee is going to be,” said Republican strategist Ford O’Connell, who served as a Trump surrogate. 

Rubio allies say it makes sense that the secretary of State be a major part of the 2028 discussion. 

New Hampshire Republican strategist Jim Merrill, who was the senior adviser for Rubio’s presidential campaign in the state, said while he expects a “robust” GOP field, “I think Secretary Rubio deserves every consideration.” 

“I’m not surprised that people are taking a long look at him right now,” he added. “Timing is a very tricky thing in politics.”

“Whether he runs or not, I think his voice is going to be incredibly important. You know, not only to the Republican Party but to the country,” Merrill said.

data.title: Raskin warns federal agencies against Signal use
data.description:
Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, warned a host of federal agencies Thursday against using apps like Signal with auto-deleting messages, writing that it violates the law and could undermine congressional oversight efforts.

The half a dozen letters to Justice Department components and various Department of Homeland Security (DHS) agencies come after the minority has come into possession of a screenshot showing the top FBI attorney corresponding with a Trump family associate on Signal.

“There is significant evidence that Trump Administration officials have engaged in the widespread destruction, mutilation, and concealment of government records, seemingly with the express purpose of circumventing federal record preservation laws,” Raskin wrote in a letter to the FBI.

“This attempt to evade transparency extends to the highest levels of federal agencies, including top-ranking law enforcement officials.”

The letters reference a Signal chat between Sam Ramer, the FBI general counsel, communicating with Drew Lynch over Signal. Lynch, a producer for Kimberly Guilfoyle, has also been sought for questioning by the House Oversight Committee as it probes the former ambassador’s solicitation of funds from a Trump ally to pay off her credit card debt ahead of her confirmation hearing.

Ramer sent Lynch a letter that had been sent to FBI Director Kash Patel referencing Abubakar Atiq Durrani, who was indicted in 2013. Their correspondence appears to include a link about Durrani being found in Pakistan in 2024. It’s unclear whether the conversation took place on Ramer’s personal or work device.

Raskin described the brief exchange as “concerning a potential or ongoing investigation involving an individual wanted by federal authorities on health care fraud and related charges. As reflected in the attached chat, the participants appear to have deliberately configured the conversation to automatically delete messages after one week.”

“It is a felony to unlawfully conceal, remove, alter, or destroy federal records, as Mr. Ramer appears to have done here,” Raskin wrote.

The FBI did not immediately respond to request for comment.

It’s not the first time the administration has been caught using Signal. Administration officials were widely criticized after accidentally including a The Atlantic reporter on a Signal group chat discussing pending military strikes against Houthis.

The letter from Raskin also asks the FBI to “open an inquiry to identify records under its purview that have been improperly deleted from non-government applications and, pursuant to 44 U.S.C. § 3106, initiate immediate action to recover these records.”

data.title: Melania Trump marks world premiere of Prime Video docuseries
data.description:
NEW YORK — Melania Trump is celebrating her docuseries debut, stepping out for a Hollywood-style premiere of “Melania: The Series.”

The first lady traded the White House for the black — rather than red — carpet on Thursday night, as she marked the forthcoming release of her two-part Prime Video series.

“You will see my beliefs, my principles, what I think about family trust, also pride and honor,” Trump told reporters.

Despite being in the spotlight for years, Trump told ITK in an interview that some of the public still has misconceptions about her.

“People they don’t really want to know, maybe, or they don’t focus on what I do,” Trump said. “They prefer to gossip, and they go in [a] different direction. And if they see what I do, I think it would be much more important.”

The series, to be released on Friday, has been touted by Prime Video as a project that offers audiences “an intimate look” at the 56-year-old author and former model as she navigates stepping into the role of first lady again in 2025 following President Trump’s second inauguration. The first episode is focused on family and trust, while the second part of the series, titled “Pride and Honor,” explores “the immediate responsibilities of serving as first lady.”

The release of the docuseries comes nearly a year after Trump made her documentary film debut. “Melania,” which reportedly cost Amazon MGM Studios $75 million, followed the first lady in the days before the 2025 presidential inauguration. The film reportedly grossed more than $16 million after it was released in January.

Amid the President Trump’s low approval rating and the GOP’s crushing losses in the midterm elections, it’s unclear if there’s an appetite for more first lady-focused fare.

But Marc Beckman, Melania Trump’s exclusive senior adviser, said that now was the right time for the first lady to share her story.

“I think it was a result of, for years and years, people asking her to see more, to understand more, and this is the truth,” Beckman said. “So you see a person that’s hardworking, committed to her family, committed to foster care children and children all over the world, and she opens this up to the world.”

The premiere at New York’s Lincoln Center drew a gathering of figures from all avenues of Trump’s life: “Melania” director Brett Ratner, fashion designer Hervé Pierre — who helped craft her inaugural gowns — and former Attorney General Pam Bondi, among others, all on-hand for the event. President Trump, who traveled back to the U.S. on Thursday following summits as well as bilateral and trilateral meetings in Asia, did not attend the event.

While her series will soon premiere on Prime Video, Trump said she doesn’t binge watch any shows herself.

“I don’t have time. I’m reading some executive orders actually, so maybe we pass some more,” she said, noting her work on women’s health and her Fostering the Future initiative.

“My time here is now. I want to focus here now, and let’s see what the future brings,” she said.

When asked by ITK if she’ll miss Washington when the president leaves office, Trump — who splits her time between the nation’s capital, Palm Beach, Fla., and New York — replied, “We love D.C. We love the White House. It’s a beautiful place.”

And what might the post-White House future hold for Trump?

“It’s too early to say,” she said with a smile.

data.title: Army postpones controlled lead detonation after pleas from Iowa lawmakers
data.description:
Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle announced he would be postponing Friday’s detonations of lead azide barrels in Iowa amid heavy pushback from lawmakers who say they were given short notice about the planned explosions. 

“Public safety is the Army’s top priority, and I have directed Army Materiel Command to postpone tomorrow’s controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa until Monday, November 23,” Telle wrote on social media. 

He continued that delaying the explosion until Monday would be “the latest possible moment” before a forecasted temperature drop would further destabilize parts of the lead azide, which are typically used as explosives for secondary bombs.

The acting Army secretary said the lead azide was first discovered in March and started working immediately with “stakeholders and the public in Middletown and the modeled impact area about the danger it posed.”

“In coordination with the Environmental Protection Agency, experts, and the local community, it was determined that a controlled detonation was the option that posed the lowest risk to the public in the immediate and surrounding area,” he stated. “Therefore, the Army will continue to actively engage with state and local officials throughout the region to distribute accurate, up-to-date information.”

The Army announced the detonation in a Nov. 15 press release. Nearby residents were asked to vacate the area from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. local time on Friday before its delay.

“While safety measures will be fully enforced, the controlled detonation will cause temporary noise, ground vibrations, and a dust plume that will contain some lead,” the release said. “Residents in Middletown will hear a loud noise; feel vibrations from two consecutive, rapid detonations; and will see a plume of dust.”

Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand (D) expressed that “an unacceptable lack of communication and clarity” had made Iowans stressed about the situation. 

Sen.-elect Josh Turek (D-Iowa) stated that it was “deeply troubling” the Army didn’t give prior notice to outgoing Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds (R) or other public officials. Outgoing Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) similarly remarked that she believed surrounding communities “were not given adequate notice.”

data.title: Russell Brand's crimes were an 'open secret':  Why didn't anyone stop him?
data.description:
Editor’s Note: This story contains discussions of rape or sexual assault that may be disturbing. Reader discretion is advised. If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, you can find help and discreet resources on the National Sexual Assault Hotline website or by calling 1-800-656-4673.

(NewsNation) — Russell Brand seemingly once had it all until it came crashing down in the last few weeks after he was convicted of rape and sexual assault by a U.K. jury.

The conviction and sentencing — the comedian was given 10.5 years — may have been the first time the public even heard about the controversy surrounding him, but Brand’s behavior was apparently well-known in Hollywood.

Stakeholders also protected the actor, which begs the question: Why is the same industry that protected Brand and other men, like Harvey Weinstein, making projects about them?

Following his sentencing, Netflix released the documentary “Russell Brand: Open Secret,” which reflects on his past, but also discusses how his fellow comedians used to speak about the salacious and criminal things he was accused of doing.

Brand’s predatory persona was the act itself for all these years. It appeared in his stand-up, his radio show and his films, which makes me wonder whether the public found it harder to take the allegations against him seriously.

“It 100% helped him. I think that his public persona. He’s this sexual guy, he’s outrageous, he’s deliberately inappropriate, he’s so funny,” Los Angeles Magazine contributor Lauren Conlin told me.

She adds, “It just gave him this remarkable amount of cover. Some people would just say, ‘Oh, you know, that’s just that’s Russell being Russell.’”

The “Get Him to the Greek” actor took his sexual predation as a “joke,” says Conlin, who says Brand believed his fame protected him.

No one would speak

Daniel Sloth was the only comedian who would go on record about the allegations and how the accusations had been well-known in comedy for years.

Yet even after news broke about Brand, many people weren’t willing to speak up.

“I think it’s tough just because these industries are actually small,” said Conlin. “They hear these things thirdhand,” and may not speak about it because it isn’t something they’ve directly experienced.

“Some people also just want to mind their own business,” she said. “I am wondering who else is going to come out and be like, look, I should have said something.’’

From Hollywood to the royal family, “The Scoop” delivers smart, insider revelations on celebrity news, scandals, style and culture with Paula Froelich. Subscribe to her newsletter here.

data.title: Family of Robb Elementary victim hope their experience inspires mass casualty preparedness at hospitals
data.description:
ROUND ROCK, Texas (Nexstar) — Javier Cazares wiped away the tears streaming down his face.

His wife, Gloria, is seated next to him and hands him a couple of tissues. The duo just relived the darkest day of their lives for a room full of first responders from around the country.

Javier choked up as he spoke about the moment he and his family identified the body of their nine-year-old daughter, Jackie. She was one of the 19 students who was shot and killed by an 18-year-old gunman at Robb Elementary in Uvalde.

Javier said he lifted the sheet that covered his daughter’s body, curious to see what injury killed her. “She had one single shot. A bullet wound to the chest,” Javier said through tears.

“I played that last moment over and over in my head. Was she scared? What were her final thoughts,” Gloria said about her daughter’s last moments alive as she remained trapped in the classroom for more than a hour with the gunman, as more than 300 law enforcement officers stood outside.

The Cazareses were not in Round Rock to recount the failures of law enforcement that day. They were invited to the annual convention of the Advanced Law Enforcement Rapid Response Training (ALERRT) center. Their mission this week was to talk about their concerns with the medical care Jackie received after the gunman was killed, and why it is important that EMS, police, and fire collaborate with local hospitals to create procedures on what to do in a mass casualty event.

“What we’re trying to do is get people to understand and to learn the lesson, not just our police officers, but also the health care team that’s going to take care of our children after a traumatic event,” Gloria explained.

Javier said there was no communication from medical professionals at the hospital their daughter was taken to after the shooting. The family said they waited four hours before being asked to identify Jackie’s body.

Gloria said the chest seal used on Jackie’s body at the school was too large and did not fit properly. She added that the stretcher was too big for Jackie and that her daughter almost fell off it as she was being wheeled to an ambulance.

ALERRT is the gold standard of training law enforcement agencies across the country on active shooter events. But the center is pushing hospitals to have a plan in place for a possible mass casualty event, where a hospital can quickly become overwhelmed by multiple gun shot victims.

“Those hospitals that are prepared, those are going to be the ones where people are going to survive, and they’re not going to become overwhelmed,” James Keith, the director for external affairs at the ALERRT Center, said.

In 2025, former Uvalde Mayor Don McLaughlin passed a bill as a state representative in the 89th session to mandate ALERRT training for law enforcement agencies in Texas. ALERRT said it is not looking for a similar mandate for hospitals at this time, but it hopes the Cazares’ story will inspire action from hospital systems and law enforcement.

“Jackie wasn’t just another number,” Gloria said. “She was a little girl that had dreams and she should have had a bright future. And they talk a lot about the ‘why’ here, and hopefully Jackie can be somebody’s why.”

data.title: DOJ looks to dismiss Alaska Senate lawsuit
data.description:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) is looking to dismiss its lawsuit that was focused on blocking the certification of Alaska’s Senate race if Sen.-elect Mary Peltola (D) won, according to Thursday court filings. 

This case centered on the DOJ’s anger over the presence of a spoiler candidate who shared the same name as incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska). It was decided by U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason on Nov. 1 that Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., the third-party candidate, could appear on November ballots after he advanced to Alaska’s four-candidate ranked-choice election.

DOJ attorneys argued in new court documents that the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals should overrule the previous dismissal of their case in order to effectively remove its loss but still urged the federal court to dismiss the case.

“This Court should hold that this case is moot, vacate the underlying order, and remand for dismissal on that ground,” the lawyers wrote. 

“For Alaskans, there is only one direction: forward,” Peltola told The Hill in a statement. “Now that the election is over and the voters sent a very clear message about the direction they want our state to go in, I’m eager to move forward and get to work on behalf of all Alaskans.”

The Hill’s partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) projected Peltola’s victory over Dan Sullivan, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. and Republican Gerald Heikes on Wednesday.

The DOJ’s case was filed before the New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign and national Democrats were allegedly involved in an effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan. Federal probes into the matter were launched, though Peltola denied any knowledge of the plan.

President Trump demanded in October that Peltola be removed from the race and stated he believed Alaskan voters would get confused between either Dan Sullivan. 

When the race was called by DDHQ, Peltola was still in the lead even if the votes for the senator and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. were combined, with 94 percent of the votes counted.

data.title: Senate approves key permitting reform bill, sends to House
data.description:
The Senate on Thursday passed a major bill that seeks to speed up the buildout of the nation’s energy and infrastructure — taking a massive step toward the bill becoming law.

The vote was passed by a vote of 62-33.

The bill, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), seeks to address longstanding complaints from various industries that it takes too long to build in the U.S.

Its supporters say the bill will help the U.S. economy by allowing a much faster buildout of infrastructure, including on energy. They argue that through benefits to renewable power, the legislation will also bring down the nation’s planet-warming emissions.

Opponents say that the bill would be bad for the environment as it bolsters fossil fuels and mining, loosens environmental laws and limits the ability of a project’s opponents to challenge it in court.

The legislation now heads to the House, where it’s also expected to have significant bipartisan support – although Democrats are split on the legislation. The White House is backing the legislation, and it has issued a statement of support saying the bill “would remove major obstacles to building the infrastructure we need in this country.”

In the House, the Democratic caucus is divided on the bill, with progressives opposing it on environmental grounds while many more moderate members have expressed support. Meanwhile, the bill also appears to have significant Republican support – although at least one powerful Republican has said he’d like to see some changes to the legislation. 

It also contends with a crowded lame duck calendar, including the potential for a lapse in federal funding without congressional action.

The bill aims to improve the nation’s ability to build power lines, which is key to helping renewable energy projects get onto the grid, including by allowing federal regulators to approve the lines if states don’t act on them.

It also contains provisions that seek to prevent presidents from yanking existing permits from energy of all types — combating President Trump’s ability to block already-approved wind projects and moves made by Democratic presidents, such as revoking approval from the Keystone XL pipeline.

It also allows project developers to sue the government if they can demonstrate a pattern of disparate treatment of certain energy sources. 

BAAJA also exempts certain activities, including expansions to natural gas pipelines, from environmental reviews and limits those reviews to only alternatives that meet the goal of a project’s sponsor company. 

It additionally restricts lawsuits against projects by mandating that they be filed within 150 days of a project’s approval and only allows people who weighed in during a formal public comment period to sue.

And it seeks to rein in increased electricity costs from large data centers, forcing them to pay for any costs stemming from their high electricity demand. However, these facilities may also benefit from the general provisions that seek to help industry build.
